paras: The killing of Levi Bolden took place on the morning of July 24, 1881, in the county jail at Paducah, Kentucky, where the jailer and county officials shot Bolden, a Black prisoner awaiting transfer to the penitentiary. According to the officers, Bolden had just beaten his cellmate John Stewart to death and attacked them when they opened the cell. A coroner's jury upheld the shooting the same day, and the story of the jail "tragedy" ran in papers across the country into August.

Bolden and Stewart, both described as Black, had shared a cell in the Paducah jail for ten months. The Chicago Tribune's Paducah correspondent and the Hickman Courier reported that Bolden had been sentenced to four years in the Frankfort penitentiary for highway robbery and Stewart to eighteen months for larceny, while the wire dispatch said both had been "convicted of larceny." About three months earlier, according to these accounts, Stewart had given away an attempt by Bolden to saw his way out, and Bolden had sworn revenge. Eleven convicts were to leave for the penitentiary at 8 o'clock that morning, and friends had gathered at the jail to say goodbye.

Between 6 and 7 o'clock, cries of "murder" from the cell brought Jailer Edwards, his assistant Jackson and County Judge McGannagill, who lived nearby. They found Stewart dead or dying on the floor and Bolden holding a bar from an iron bunk, which he refused to give up. When the cell was opened, Bolden swung at the jailer, missed him, and struck the deputy, knocking him down.

Accounts of the shooting differ in detail. The Chicago Tribune said three shots were heard as Bolden turned on the officials in the jail corridor, while the Hickman Courier said McGonnagill and Edwards both fired. The Clarksville Chronicle wrote that the deputy's revolver went off as it fell and that the jailer and county judge fired at almost the same moment. Bolden was hit through the body near the navel and through the head, and he died instantly.

A coroner's jury returned a verdict "in accordance with the above facts", justifying the shooting, and both men were buried that afternoon in the county cemetery. The sheriff then left for Frankfort with the nine remaining prisoners. The wire dispatch said that "all classes, white and black" thought the shooting justifiable and that there was "no excitement." By contrast, the Tribune's correspondent wrote that hundreds visited the scene and that the County Judge had to explain the shooting to an excited crowd in the Court-House yard, printed as "excited blocks" and probably "blacks", before it would disperse. No report of further legal action appears in the coverage.

A special from Paducah to the Louisville Courier-Journal was carried on July 25 by the Evening Star, the Chicago Daily Tribune, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the National Republican, and over the next days by the Memphis Appeal, the Yankton Press and Daily Dakotaian and the Stark County Democrat. Their headlines set the tone: "Killed by Officers in Self Defense" in St. Paul, "The Usual Kentucky Tragedy" in Washington and "Escaped the Penitentiary" in Memphis.

The fullest accounts came from the Chicago Tribune's own Paducah dispatch and from regional weeklies in Hickman, Kentucky, and Clarksville, Tennessee. The Tribune called Bolden "a treacherous and hardened prisoner" and Stewart "quiet and inoffensive," and the Clarksville paper set the case in a "carnival of crime" that it blamed on the hot weather. Every version of the shooting came from the officers' side, and none questioned it.

Syndicated one-sentence briefs carried the story into August in Missouri, Indiana, Arkansas, New Jersey, Wisconsin and South Carolina, sometimes naming him "Levi Borden" and saying he was killed by "a guard". The Superior Times placed the jail at Louisville and called Bolden "the infuriated black."
The same-day dispatches date the killing to July 24, matching the Clarksville paper's "last Sunday," while the Hickman Courier said Monday and the Memphis Appeal's weekly summary said Saturday.

reader.title: Killing of Levi Bolden
bases: Levi Bolden, a Black convict in the Paducah county jail, was shot dead by the jailer and other county officials after he had killed his cellmate and, by their account, attacked them (A1, A7, A10, A13).

The Courier-Journal wire dispatch (A1), a separate Paducah special to the Chicago Tribune (A7), and the Kentucky and Tennessee accounts in the Hickman Courier (A10) and Clarksville Chronicle (A13) agree that officers shot Bolden in the jail after he killed John Stewart, though every version of the shooting is the officers'.

accounts.label: Courier-Journal wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Officers found Bolden had killed Stewart; when the cell was opened he attacked them and their pistols, 'firing almost together', killed him; the coroner's jury agreed and feeling was that the shooting was justified.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune Paducah special
accounts.gist: Bolden killed Stewart in revenge for exposing an escape attempt, refused to come out, struck at the jailer, knocked down the deputy, and fell to three shots in the corridor; the inquest justified the shooting and the County Judge calmed an excited crowd.

accounts.label: Hickman Courier
accounts.gist: Bolden refused to give up his weapon and knocked Jackson down; McGonnagill and Edwards both shot him; the coroner's jury exonerated the officer.

accounts.label: Clarksville Chronicle
accounts.gist: Bolden swung at the jailer and struck the deputy, whose revolver fell and went off; the jailor and county judge then fired.

framing.detail: The wire reported that the officers would have been killed 'but for their pistols' and that all classes thought the shooting 'justifiable'; the St. Paul Globe headed it 'Killed by Officers in Self Defense'.
The Chicago Tribune called Bolden 'a treacherous and hardened prisoner' and Stewart 'quiet and inoffensive'.
Regional papers treated it as a 'Double Killing' or 'Double Tragedy'; the Clarksville paper set it in a 'carnival of crime' brought on by hot weather.
Northern and Southern papers ran short briefs, one headed 'The Usual Kentucky Tragedy' and one calling Bolden 'the infuriated black'.

versions.value: July 24 ('to-day' in dispatches dated July 24; 'yesterday' in a July 25 paper; 'on the 24th')

conflicts.note: The same-day dispatches dated July 24 are the best evidence; 'last Sunday' agrees with them; Monday and Saturday appear only in weekly summaries.

versions.value: Bolden four years for highway robbery; Stewart eighteen months for (grand) larceny

conflicts.note: The two detailed accounts give separate sentences for each man; the wire lumps them together.
